p182.lead: Thursday night on Olivet: the last group prayer with the eleven, quiet preparations before the betrayal, and the Son of Man alone in Gethsemane accepting the cup.

p182.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p182.s0.h: Introduction — From the Upper Room to the Camp
p182.s0.b0: About ten o’clock on Thursday night, Jesus led the eleven from the home of Elijah and Mary Mark back toward the Gethsemane camp. John Mark, who had been resting downstairs, heard them coming down, threw a linen coat about himself, and followed. From this time until the crucifixion he stayed close enough to witness everything and to overhear much of what the Master said.
p182.s0.b1: On the way back, the apostles for the first time suspected that something was wrong with Judas. Finding him absent from the camp, they besieged Andrew, who could only say that he did not know where Judas was but feared he had deserted them. The paper tells this tense night in three scenes.

head: Section
Scene
Key point
rows: The last group prayer
A prayer for the apostles kneeling in a circle, as on the day of their ordination
The last hour before the betrayal
Nine armed apostles, a message to Abner, and the watch kept by David and John Mark
Alone in Gethsemane
Three prayers, three sleeping apostles, and the hour when his humanity laid hold on his divinity

p182.s1.h: I. The Last Group Prayer — That They May Be One
p182.s1.b0: Jesus led the apostles a short way up Olivet to a large flat rock in full view of Jerusalem and had them kneel in a circle about him, as they had done on the day of their ordination. Then, standing in the moonlight, he lifted his eyes to heaven and prayed. The prayer has three parts: for himself, for the eleven, and for all who would come to believe through their word.

head: Prayed for
Main petitions
rows: The Son himself
Glorify me with the glory I had with you before this world was, and receive me once more at your right hand
The eleven
Do not take them out of the world but keep them from the evil in it; sanctify them in the truth
All who will believe
That they may be one, as the Father and the Son are one, and love one another

p182.s1.b3: In the first part of the prayer, Jesus acknowledged that he had exalted the Father on earth and accomplished the work given him, and that only the laying down of his life in the flesh remained. He told the Father that he had manifested him to the men chosen out of the world, and that they were learning that all he had came from the Father. As he had represented the Father in this world, so they would now represent him. When the prayer ended, the eleven remained kneeling for several minutes and then went back to the camp in silence.
p182.s1.b4: The prayer for the apostles is full of trust. Jesus said they were weak and frail, but that they could be trusted, and that he had kept them all save one, the son of revenge, who would not have further fellowship. He knew there was no need to ask the Father to watch over them, yet he asked, so that the apostles might better realize that the Father loves them as the Son does.
p182.s1.b6: The narrator stresses that Jesus prayed for unity but did not desire uniformity. Sin creates a dead level of evil inertia, but righteousness nourishes the creative spirit of individual experience in living truth. In the believer’s spiritual fellowship with the Father, then, there can be no doctrinal finality or sectarian superiority. This reminds communities of faith not to mistake oneness for thinking the same thoughts in the same forms.
p182.s1.b8: In the course of the prayer Jesus said that he had manifested the Father’s name to the world. The text contrasts this with the revelation in the time of Moses, when the Father could proceed no further than “I AM.” But by the end of Jesus’ earth life, that name had been so fully revealed that he could speak of himself in sixteen “I am” sayings.

head: Theme
The “I am” sayings
rows: Giver of life
The bread of life; the living water; the reality of endless life; the resurrection and the life
Opener of the way
The open door to eternal salvation; the pathway of infinite perfection; the way, the truth, and the life
Guide and light
The light of the world; the good shepherd; the true vine
Hope and mystery
The desire of all ages; the secret of eternal survival; the hope of all who know the living truth
Connector
The living bridge from one world to another; the living link between time and eternity
Revealer of the Father
The infinite Father of my finite children

p182.s2.h: II. The Last Hour Before the Betrayal — Each in His Place
p182.s2.b0: David Zebedee and John Mark told Jesus they had kept Judas under observation for several days and knew what he intended. Jesus only replied that nothing could happen to the Son of Man unless the Father so willed. His cheerfulness was waning, and he grew more serious, even sorrowful. He sent the apostles to their tents, asking only Peter, James, and John to stay with him.
p182.s2.b2: Before sleeping, Simon Zelotes handed out the swords stored in his tent. Only Nathaniel refused to arm himself, saying that the Master’s kingdom was not of this world and his disciples should not fight with the sword. He would pray, he said, but he would not wield the sword. Hearing this, Andrew handed his sword back, and so nine of them were armed as they parted for the night.
p182.s2.b4: For a while, resentment that Judas was a traitor eclipsed everything else in the apostles’ minds; the Master’s reference to Judas in the last prayer had opened their eyes. Ordinarily they would have bidden him a personal good night, but that evening, overcome by the shock and by the weight of the farewell prayer, they went away in silence. Still, they expected any arrest to come early in the morning, since no secular work was done after noon on the preparation day for the Passover. Only David and John Mark knew Judas was coming that very night.
p182.s2.b5: To the end, Jesus remembered those far away. He sent Jacob, David’s fleetest messenger, to Abner at Philadelphia with word that he would be put to death but would rise and appear to him before going to the Father. He forewarned the chief of the Greeks encamped with them in the same way and told him to strengthen his brethren. And he asked Andrew to keep the brethren together until he came again.
p182.s2.b6: David took the watch on the upper trail toward the Bethany road, and John Mark on the road by the Kidron. In saying farewell, David told Jesus that though he was not an apostle, he had delighted to do the lesser things as they should be done. Jesus answered that others had done what they were directed to do, but David had served from his own heart. David also told him that Jesus’ family was in Jericho that night and would arrive early the next morning.
p182.s3.h: III. Alone in Gethsemane — Not My Will, but Yours
p182.s3.b0: When the camp was quiet, Jesus took the three apostles up a nearby ravine where he often prayed. They had never seen their Master so heavy-laden. He told them to watch with him and went about a stone’s throw away, fell on his face, and prayed three times. Each time he returned, he found the three asleep. John Mark, who had left his post to follow, saw and heard it all from the bushes.

head: Prayer
Jesus’ petition
What followed
rows: First
He does not shrink from death, but would know that drinking this cup is the Father’s will
The three were asleep: “can you not watch with me even for one hour?”
Second
He knows the cup can be avoided, but would drink it if it is the Father’s will
A mighty angel came and strengthened him; the apostles slept again
Third
Have mercy on my apostles; not my will, but yours, be done
“The time of decision is past”; the betrayer was at hand

p182.s3.b3: The narrator reads this scene as new evidence of Jesus’ humanity. Before the greatest revelation of his divinity, the resurrection, must come the greatest proofs of his mortal nature, his humiliation and crucifixion. Each time he prayed, his humanity laid a firmer faith-hold on his divinity, and his human will became more completely one with the Father’s will. The angel brought word that the Father desired his Son to finish his bestowal by passing through the experience of death, as all mortal creatures must.
p182.s3.b4: The text does not hide his anguish. He was weary from long labor and anxiety for his apostles, and the perspiration rolled off his face in great drops. Knowing how weak they were, he dreaded to leave them, and his human heart searched for some legitimate avenue of escape. When that search failed, he was willing to drink the cup. He was fully determined to use none of his sovereign power as head of a universe to save himself, and the armies of heaven had been warned not to intervene unless he ordered it.
p182.s3.b5: His suffering came less from death itself than from baffled love. He was isolated from his family in the flesh, one of his chosen associates was betraying him, and his father Joseph’s people had rejected him and so sealed their doom as a people. The divine mind of Michael knew he had done his best for the twelve, but the human heart of Jesus wished more might have been done for them before they were left alone. Any reader who knows what it is to leave loved ones behind will feel the Master very near in this passage.
p182.s3.b6: In this great sorrow his mind went back to his childhood in Nazareth and his early work in Galilee. He soothed himself with memories of Capernaum and Mount Hermon and of sunrise and sunset on the Sea of Galilee. And before Judas and the soldiers arrived, he had fully regained his customary poise.
p182.s4.b0: Paper 182 records the night when the Son of God struggled in the most human way. He prayed first for those he would leave behind, sent word even to those far away, and only then wrestled alone with his own cup. His peace came not from the absence of anguish but from passing through it and wholly committing his will to the Father’s. The reader sees that the same path lies open in the Gethsemanes of his or her own life.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Seek unity without imposing uniformity
Unity, not uniformity (182:1.8)
Ask to be kept from evil rather than taken out of the world
Keep them from the evil in the world (182:1.5)
Meet a crisis with faith rather than force
Nathaniel’s refusal (182:2.3)
Serve from the heart, not only as directed
David Zebedee’s service (182:2.10)
Bring anguish honestly to the Father in prayer
The three prayers (182:3.4)
Steady the heart with good memories and regain poise
Memories of Nazareth and Galilee (182:3.10)

p182.s4.b2: In the next paper, Paper 183, “The Betrayal and Arrest of Jesus,” Judas appears in Gethsemane leading the armed guards.
p183.lead: The night in Gethsemane, the betrayal by Judas and the arrest of Jesus: an account of the arrest read with the Father’s will kept distinct from the evil deeds of men.

p183.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p183.s0.h: Introduction — The Son of Man Waiting Alone
p183.s0.b0: After the prayers of Paper 182, Jesus woke Peter, James, and John and urged them to go to their tents and rest. But the arrival of excited messengers looking for David Zebedee stirred the camp, and only the eight apostles remained sound asleep. The Greeks, who had posted a sentinel, streamed out of their tents fully armed when the alarm was given.
p183.s0.b1: Unable to disperse his followers, Jesus left them and went down to the olive press near the entrance to Gethsemane Park. He feared that if the apostles were present at his arrest, they would resist and be taken and perhaps killed with him. He knew, too, that while the plot began in the councils of the rulers, it had the full approval of the rebels.
p183.s1.h: I. The Father’s Will — Drinking the Cup Is Not the Same as Cruelty
p183.s1.b0: Before entering the story of the arrest, trials, and death, the narrator guards against a misunderstanding. The fact that Jesus did the Father’s will in patiently enduring suffering and humiliation must not lead us to think that the actions of those who abused him were also the Father’s will. The Father’s will was that his Son should drink to the full the cup of mortal experience, from birth to death.
p183.s1.b2: The Father wanted the bestowal Son to finish his earth career naturally, as all mortals must. Just as ordinary men and women cannot expect a special dispensation to ease their last hours, Jesus chose to lay down his life in keeping with the natural outworking of events. The cruelty was willed neither by God in heaven nor dictated by Jesus’ archenemies; it was the work of thoughtless and evil mortals.

head: Aspect
What the text says
rows: The Father’s will
That the Son should drink to the full the cup of mortal experience, from birth to death
Jesus’ choice
To lay down his life in keeping with natural events, refusing to extricate himself
Men’s deeds
Torture, indignity, and unfair trials: the work of evil mortals, not the will of the Father
The rebels
Did much to have mortals reject the bestowal Son, yet even the father of sin turned his face away from the crucifixion

p183.s1.b5: This distinction matters for today’s reader as well. A faith that accepts suffering does not thereby justify the evil that caused it. Doing God’s will does not mean believing that God brought about everything that happens; it means walking on, in any circumstance, while committing oneself to the Father.
p183.s2.h: II. Judas in the City — A Plan Grown Out of Fear
p183.s2.b0: Leaving the Last Supper, Judas went with his cousin to the captain of the temple guards and offered to lead them to Jesus. But when they reached the Mark home, Jesus and the eleven had left fully fifteen minutes before and were on their way to the Olivet camp. Judas’s plan to take Jesus while the city was quiet had gone wrong.
p183.s2.b1: Judas knew that more than threescore disciples were at the camp and that Simon Zelotes had a store of arms. Afraid that the eleven would hate him and seek to destroy him, he asked for forty armed soldiers. The Jewish rulers reminded him that Jesus had always preached nonresistance, but Judas was not sure all his followers would obey that teaching. The narrator puts his inner state plainly.
p183.s2.b3: The betrayal is portrayed not as a decision of a moment but as an act that grew out of long-accumulated fear and suspicion. The more his anxiety to protect himself grew, the more Judas relied on more soldiers and tighter calculation. The passage shows how far fear can drive a person.

head: Stage
What happened
rows: The temple
Judas asked the captain of the temple guards to assemble the guards
The Mark home
Jesus and the eleven had already left; the arrest failed
The high priest’s home
The rulers were assembled; Judas asked for soldiers, citing armed followers at Gethsemane
The fortress of Antonia
The Roman commander learned the purpose and refused
Pilate’s house
Despite his wife’s request, the governor granted it at the personal request of the Sanhedrin’s presiding officer
Departure
About half past eleven, more than sixty persons set out with Judas: temple guards, Roman soldiers, and servants

p183.s2.b5: Pilate was reluctant to be involved, but he granted the petition, thinking he could later right any wrong they might commit. The text notes calmly that more than an hour was consumed going from one authority to another. It is worth remembering that this hesitation to take responsibility for a decision recurs in the trials that follow.
p183.s3.h: III. The Master’s Arrest — “I Am He”
p183.s3.b0: As the band with torches approached the garden, Judas stepped out in front. He meant to point out Jesus before the apostles could rally to his defense, and to avoid appearing connected with the armed guards. But Jesus, though he spoke to him kindly, greeted him as a traitor, and Judas was so confused that he made no attempt to flee.
p183.s3.b1: Jesus made one last effort to save Judas from actually betraying him. Before Judas could reach him, he himself asked the Roman captain whom they sought and declared his identity. At his calm majesty, those in the front ranks fell backward. There was no longer any need for Judas to betray him, yet Judas went through with his plan in order to claim the reward and honors he expected.
p183.s3.b3: The apostles and disciples were stunned. Disengaging himself from the traitorous embrace, Jesus stepped up to the guards and asked the same question again, this time adding words for the sake of his companions.
p183.s3.b5: The Roman captain was willing to let the apostles go in peace. But when Malchus, the high priest’s Syrian bodyguard, moved to bind Jesus’ hands without any order to do so, Peter drew his sword. Jesus raised a forbidding hand and stopped him.
p183.s3.b7: He could have commanded more than twelve legions of angels, but he did not. As he was bound, he asked only why they came out with swords and staves as if to seize a robber, when he had taught publicly in the temple every day. His followers fled into the ravine. John Mark, hiding in a shed, was seized by the coat by a soldier; he slipped out of the garment, escaped, and ran to tell David Zebedee.
p183.s4.h: IV. Discussion at the Olive Press — The Scattered Sheep
p183.s4.b0: After the arrest, the remaining apostles and disciples gathered at the olive press to decide what to do. Andrew, released from responsibility for managing the group, was silent. Simon Zelotes stood on the stone wall and urged them to go after the mob and rescue Jesus, but others reminded them of the teaching of nonresistance and the charge to preserve their lives.

head: Who
Position
rows: Simon Zelotes
Urged them to pursue the mob and rescue Jesus
Nathaniel
Recalled the teaching of nonresistance and the instruction to preserve their lives for preaching the gospel
James Zebedee
Supported Nathaniel, telling how Jesus bade Peter sheathe his sword
Thomas
Argued they could not save a Master who refused to be defended, and persuaded them to scatter
David Zebedee
Stayed at the camp to keep a clearinghouse and messenger headquarters

p183.s4.b2: By half past two in the morning the camp was deserted. Five apostles hid at Bethpage and Bethany, four hid in the city, and Peter and John followed to the home of Annas. As Jesus had directed, John stayed near him to the end and sent word through David’s messengers to the hiding apostles and to Jesus’ family.
p183.s4.b4: They vaguely realized that Jesus had forewarned them of this very situation, but the shock of his sudden disappearance kept them from thinking clearly. At daybreak Peter wandered back to the camp in deep despair, and David sent him with a messenger to Andrew at the home of Nicodemus. The scene honestly shows that a warning heard in advance is not easily held onto once the crisis actually comes.
p183.s4.b5: It is worth noting that even in their scattering, David Zebedee’s messenger service kept all the groups in touch. In a time of confusion, one person’s steady service can become the bond of a community. Jude, Jesus’ brother, also arrived breathless and carried the news back to the family.
p183.s5.h: V. On the Way to the High Priest’s Palace — A Place for One Friend
p183.s5.b0: Before they left the garden, the captain of the temple guards wanted to take Jesus to Caiaphas, while the Roman captain directed that he be taken to Annas. Since the Romans were in the habit of dealing with Annas on matters of Jewish ecclesiastical law, the Roman captain’s order was obeyed. Judas marched near the two captains, but neither would so much as speak to him.
p183.s5.b1: When John Zebedee came up beside Jesus, the captain of the temple guards ordered him bound, but the Roman captain protected him. He recognized John’s courage: he had not drawn a sword in the garden, yet he had come forward to be with his Master.
p183.s5.b3: Hearing this, Judas was so ashamed that he dropped behind the marchers. The Roman captain told his assistant to see that the Jews did not kill the prisoner without Pilate’s consent and that John be permitted to observe. So John could stay near Jesus up to his death on the cross, while the other ten apostles remained in hiding. One officer’s fair judgment gave one disciple a place to watch to the very end.
p183.s6.b0: Paper 183 records the night of the arrest calmly and sets two faces side by side: Judas, driven by fear into calculation after calculation, and Jesus, stepping forward himself to protect his companions. The paper teaches us to distinguish between accepting suffering and justifying evil.
p183.s6.b1: Jesus could have called legions of angels, yet he used neither sword nor miracle, and to the end he put his companions’ safety before his own. Around him were Peter with his drawn sword, the scattered apostles, David keeping the lines of communication open, and John staying by his side. The reader may ask where he or she stands among them.

head: Practice
The passage behind it
rows: Do not confuse suffering and evil with God’s will
The inhuman experiences were no part of the Father’s will (183:1.1)
Do not let fear steer your judgment
Judas’s anxiety and calculation (183:2.2)
Step forward first to protect others
“Let these others go their way” (183:3.6)
Choose nonresistance over violence
Put up your sword (183:3.7)
Be a link that holds people together in scattered times
David Zebedee’s messenger service (183:4.8)
Be a friend who stays to the end
John’s courage (183:5.3)

p183.s6.b3: In the next paper, Paper 184, “Before the Sanhedrin Court,” come the examination by Annas, Peter’s denials, and the trial before the Sanhedrin court.
p184.lead: The examination by Annas, Peter’s repeated denials in the courtyard, and a midnight court that abandoned the procedures of law, faced by the Son of Man in silence.

p184.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p184.s0.h: Introduction — The Night the Court Was Waiting
p184.s0.b0: After his arrest, Jesus was taken first to the palace of Annas, the former high priest, on Mount Olivet. Annas wanted to keep his prestige as chief ecclesiastical authority and to gain time, since the Sanhedrin court could not lawfully be convened before the morning sacrifice. Meanwhile some thirty members of the Sanhedrin were waiting at the palace of Caiaphas, ready to sit in judgment.
p184.s0.b1: The text states clearly how this court was made up. Since twenty-three members were enough to constitute a trial court, only those strongly and openly opposed to Jesus were summoned. The trial this paper describes should be read with that in mind: it was not the decision of a whole people but a proceeding hastily arranged by a particular few.
p184.s0.b3: John Zebedee could move freely in the palace not only because of the Roman captain’s word, but also because Annas was a distant relative of his mother, Salome, and the older servants knew him well.
p184.s1.h: I. Examination by Annas — To One Who Knowingly Rejects the Light
p184.s1.b0: Enriched by the temple revenues, father-in-law of the acting high priest, and well connected with the Roman authorities, Annas was the most powerful single individual in all Jewry. He wanted the trial kept in the hands of the Sadducees. What had stirred his enmity most was not Jesus’ teaching but the threat to his revenues when Jesus drove the money-changers out of the temple.
p184.s1.b1: At first Annas thought he might persuade Jesus to abandon his claims and leave Palestine, for he was reluctant to take part in the murder of a good man. But before the Master’s majesty and poise, he soon saw that such proposals were useless. Jesus made no reply when asked the names of his disciples, and when Annas pointed to his power over the coming trial, Jesus answered him this way.
p184.s1.b3: Asked about his teaching, Jesus said he had spoken openly to the world, so Annas should ask those who had heard him. At that the chief steward struck him in the face, and Annas spoke no word of rebuke. Jesus did not strike back; he answered with a fair question.
p184.s1.b5: Asked whether he was the Messiah, Jesus said he claimed nothing except what his Father had appointed, and that he had been sent to all men, gentile as well as Jew. As daybreak neared, Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas.
p184.s1.b6: When Annas asked once more whether he had claimed to be the Messiah, Jesus looked at him and replied only, “⟦Q 184:1.8⟧So you have said.⟦/Q⟧” Even before a man who had known him since his youth, he neither made excuses nor pleaded. This bearing, neither lowering nor exalting himself before the powerful, shows the dignity an honest person can keep under threat.
p184.s2.h: II. Peter in the Courtyard — The First Step of Compromise
p184.s2.b0: At John’s request, the portress let Peter into the courtyard of Annas. Having thrown away his sword, Peter warmed himself by the charcoal fire. The text says he was out of place there. Jesus had told only John to stay near at hand and had specifically warned the other apostles not to endanger their lives.

head: Order
Who asked
Peter’s answer
rows: First
The portress: “Are you not also one of this man’s disciples?”
“I am not.”
Second
Another servant: did I not see you in the garden?
“I know not this man, neither am I one of his followers.”
Third
The portress: my sister saw you in the temple
Denied all knowledge of Jesus with cursing and swearing
Fourth
A man near the fire: your Galilean speech betrays you
Again denied all connection
Fifth
The gate-keeper and her sister
Denied once more, and the cock crowed

p184.s2.b2: When the cock crowed, Peter remembered the Master’s warning. Just then Jesus, being led to Caiaphas, turned and looked at him. Peter never forgot that look as long as he lived.
p184.s2.b4: Peter sat down by the roadside and wept bitterly. The narrator adds that until the cock crowed, Peter had been congratulating himself on how cleverly he had eluded the servants’ accusations. Then the text explains why a wrong path, once entered, is so hard to leave.
p184.s2.b6: Peter never fully believed he could be forgiven until, after the resurrection, he saw that the Master received him just as before. The comfort this scene leaves the reader is that the look of love is not withdrawn even after failure.
p184.s3.h: III. Before the Court of Sanhedrists — Silence as Refutation
p184.s3.b0: At half past three on Friday morning, Caiaphas called the court of inquiry to order in the high priest’s palace. This was not a regular meeting of the Sanhedrin held in its usual place in the temple but a special court of some thirty members. The text notes that ordinary Jewish trials on capital charges proceeded with great caution and every safeguard of fairness, yet on this occasion Caiaphas was more a prosecutor than a judge.
p184.s3.b2: Jewish law required at least two witnesses to agree, but the testimony of more than a score of false witnesses was so contradictory that the Sanhedrists themselves were ashamed. The nearest thing to agreement concerned a saying about destroying the temple and building another in three days, and even that was not exactly what Jesus had said.
p184.s3.b3: Judas could not be a witness, because Jewish law forbade the testimony of a traitor. Jesus looked down benignly on the perjurers and answered not a word. Their testimony, full of hatred and exaggeration, fell in its own entanglements.

head: Charge argued by Annas
Substance
rows: A dangerous traducer of the people
He taught them impossible things and otherwise deceived them
A fanatical revolutionist
He advocated laying violent hands on the sacred temple
A teacher of magic
He promised to build a new temple without hands

p184.s3.b6: The Sanhedrin had already agreed that Jesus deserved death for transgressing Jewish law. What concerned them now was framing charges that would justify Pilate in pronouncing a death sentence, since the governor’s consent was needed for a lawful execution. Annas set out to make Jesus appear a dangerous teacher to have abroad among the people.
p184.s3.b7: Unable to endure the Master’s silence, Caiaphas adjured him in the name of the living God to say whether he was the Son of God. To this question alone, the one concerning his bestowal mission, Jesus answered instantly and unequivocally in the affirmative. The high priest tore his garments and cried blasphemy, and the first session ended at half past four in disorder, with spitting and blows.
p184.s4.h: IV. The Hour of Humiliation — The Greatest Victory
p184.s4.b0: Jewish law required two sessions of the court for a death sentence, with a day of fasting and mourning between them. This court waited only one hour. During that hour the guards and servants mocked Jesus, spat on him, and struck him. Fearing that John’s indignation would cost him his life, Jesus signaled him with a nod to withdraw.
p184.s4.b1: The narrator asks here about the brutality that still lurks in man: the urge to insult and assault what one cannot spiritually attain. But Jesus, though undefending, was not defenseless, and he was not vanquished.
p184.s4.b4: The text sees this moment as the final triumph over all fears of creature personality isolation. Jesus asserts without hesitation that he and the Father are one, and he urges believers to become one with him in the same way. In this way the God-knowing believer is delivered from the isolation of the self and comes to experience the joy of spiritual socialization on a universe scale.
p184.s4.b5: In the middle of this record of suffering, the passage sets out a promise for the believer’s life. Loneliness and fear, with the helplessness that comes with them, form the deepest prison a person can know. In the loneliest place of all Jesus held fast to his oneness with the Father, and the text says that this experience becomes a sure way for believers to escape their isolation.
p184.s5.h: V. The Second Meeting of the Court — Charges for Pilate
p184.s5.b0: The court reassembled at half past five to draw up the charges to be presented to Pilate. Annas pointed out that a charge of blasphemy would carry no weight with Pilate. In half an hour a three-part indictment was complete.

head: Count
Allegation
rows: A perverter of the Jewish nation who deceived the people and incited them to rebellion
Taught the people to refuse to pay tribute to Caesar
By claiming to be a king and founder of a new kind of kingdom, incited treason against the emperor

p184.s5.b2: The text judges the whole procedure irregular and wholly contrary to Jewish law. No two witnesses had agreed on any matter of substance, no witnesses spoke for the defense, and there was not even a formal ballot on blasphemy. Worth noting too is the record that three Pharisees took their leave rather than formulate charges without witnesses and in the prisoner’s absence.
p184.s5.b3: Those who had judged a sinless life did not want to look on his face again. At six o’clock in the morning Jesus was led out to appear before Pilate for confirmation of the death sentence.
p184.s5.b4: Meanwhile some women of the palace came to look at the strange prisoner and asked whether he was the Messiah. Jesus answered that if he told them they would not believe, and if he asked them they would not answer. This short reply shows that a question seeking truth is different from mere curiosity.
p184.s6.b0: Moving between the midnight court and the courtyard fire, Paper 184 shows two kinds of failure: a few judges who tore down due process to protect their power and interests, and a beloved apostle who denied his Master out of fear. In the midst of them stood Jesus, enduring everything with silence and a few words of truth, and loving even them.

p184.s6.b2: In the next paper, Paper 185, “The Trial Before Pilate,” the hearings continue before the Roman governor, together with the examination by Herod.
p185.lead: Jesus before Pilate and Herod: a judge who asked about truth yet gave in to fear, and a king who answered with silence and brief testimony.

p185.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p185.s0.h: Introduction — Six O’Clock on Friday Morning
p185.s0.b0: A little after six o’clock on the morning of Friday, April 7, A.D. 30, Jesus was brought, his hands bound, before Pontius Pilate, the Roman procurator who governed Judea, Samaria, and Idumea. About fifty accusers went with him, among them Caiaphas and other members of the Sanhedrist court, together with Judas, and the Apostle John also came along. Annas did not appear.
p185.s0.b1: The public hearing took place on the steps outside the governor’s headquarters, because the accusers refused to enter a gentile building on the day of preparation for the Passover; doing so would have made them ceremonially unclean. The narrator points out the contradiction of men who plotted a judicial murder while remaining scrupulous about ritual cleanness, and then adds that they were not the only ones to fall into it.
p185.s0.b3: This sentence is a key to the whole paper. The narrative records the failings of particular people, but it widens those failings into a trap that all human beings can easily fall into. Keeping the form while missing the substance can happen to religious people of any age.
p185.s1.h: I. Pontius Pilate — Capable, but a Moral Coward
p185.s1.b0: Pilate was a fairly good administrator, good enough to hold his post for ten years, yet the text calls him a moral coward. He never grasped that the people he governed had a real religion, a faith for which they were willing to die. Having lost prestige through his early blunders, he gave way again and again before the threat of revolt.

head: Incident
What happened
Outcome
rows: The image of Caesar on the ensigns
Troops entered Jerusalem bearing the images; Pilate refused petitions for five days and threatened death
He yielded before men ready to die — shown up as one who made threats he dared not carry out
The emperor’s shields in Herod’s palace
Hoping to regain prestige, he hung the shields and ignored protests
The matter was appealed to Rome, and the emperor ordered them removed
The temple treasury and the aqueduct
He tried to build an aqueduct with temple funds
More than a score of riots and much bloodshed
The Mount Gerizim affair
He slaughtered Samaritans following a false Messiah
Recalled to Rome, never reinstated, and he died at Lausanne

p185.s1.b3: The text tells us that Pilate never fully recovered from regret and guilt over having consented to the crucifixion of Jesus. His wife, Claudia Procula, had heard of Jesus through her Phoenician maid, a believer in the gospel, and after her husband’s death she gave herself to spreading the good news.
p185.s1.b4: The narrator remarks that a good procurator would not have allowed a man he had declared innocent to be put to death, and he judges that it was a great mistake for Rome to send a second-rate governor to Judea. It is a sober reminder of how far the moral courage of a single person can reach.
p185.s2.h: II. Jesus Appears Before Pilate — A Death Sentence Without a Charge
p185.s2.b0: When Pilate asked what charge they brought, the accusers only replied that they would not have delivered this man if he were not an evildoer. They wanted nothing more than confirmation of a sentence. Pilate tried to send them back to judge Jesus by their own law, and he took some pleasure in making them admit publicly that they had no authority to put anyone to death.
p185.s2.b2: The written charges handed over by the clerk accused Jesus of perverting the nation and stirring up rebellion, of forbidding the people to pay tribute to Caesar, and of calling himself a king and teaching a new kingdom. The text stresses that Jesus had never been regularly tried or legally convicted on any of these charges. When the indictment was read, Jesus made no reply.
p185.s2.b3: Pilate was astonished at the unfairness of the proceedings, and he was deeply stirred by the way Jesus looked down upon his accusers. There was no scorn in that look. It held deep pity and sorrowful affection.
p185.s3.h: III. The Private Examination by Pilate — “What Is Truth?”
p185.s3.b0: Pilate took Jesus and John into a private room, had them sit down, and questioned the prisoner. He said plainly that he did not believe the first charge. On the question of tribute, John testified that Jesus and his apostles had paid taxes both to Caesar and to the temple. On the third charge — was he a king? — Jesus explained the nature of his kingdom.

head: Charge in the indictment
What the private examination showed
rows: Perverting the nation and stirring up rebellion
Pilate said from the outset that he did not believe it
Forbidding tribute to Caesar
John’s testimony — Jesus and the apostles had paid taxes to both Caesar and the temple
Calling himself king of the Jews
Jesus’ kingdom is not of this world: a spiritual dominion, the brotherhood of the faith sons of God

p185.s3.b3: Jesus said that his standing before Pilate in bonds was enough to show that his kingdom was a spiritual dominion. It is the brotherhood of men who, through faith and by love, have become the sons of God, and it is open to the gentile as much as to the Jew. Then he declared the purpose for which he had been born: to show the Father to all men and to bear witness to the truth of God.
p185.s3.b5: Half in ridicule and half in sincerity, Pilate asked what truth was. He could not understand a spiritual kingdom, but he was sure the prisoner had done nothing deserving death. He went out and announced that he found no crime in him. Yet when he heard that Jesus had begun his work in Galilee, he seized the chance to escape responsibility and sent him to Herod.
p185.s4.h: IV. Jesus Before Herod — A King Who Wanted a Show
p185.s4.b0: Herod Antipas was very curious about Jesus and hoped to see a miracle with his own eyes. He did not recognize the man before him as the lad who long before had come to plead for a just settlement of the compensation owed for his father’s accidental death at Sepphoris. For about fifteen minutes he questioned and mocked Jesus, but Jesus did not answer a single word.
p185.s4.b1: In the end Herod jeered at Jesus, put an old purple royal robe on him, and sent him back to Pilate. He knew he had no jurisdiction in Judea, and he was relieved that the responsibility for any execution would rest with Pilate. The fear that had haunted him since he killed John the Baptist also eased when he saw that Jesus was a very different kind of man.
p185.s4.b2: Jesus’ complete silence before Herod deserves attention. To Pilate, who asked with some sincerity, he explained his kingdom; to Herod, who wanted the spectacle of a miracle, he showed nothing at all. Truth is not a tool for satisfying curiosity; it is given to the heart that seeks it.
p185.s5.h: V. Jesus Returns to Pilate — Between Barabbas and Jesus
p185.s5.b0: Pilate announced once more that Herod had reached the same conclusion, that Jesus had done nothing worthy of death, and that he would chastise him and release him. Just then a crowd arrived asking for the customary Passover release of a prisoner. Pilate saw this as a way out of his difficulty, but the crowd shouted the name of Barabbas, a political agitator and murderous robber.
p185.s5.b1: The text explains why the crowd turned. When Jesus drove the traders from the temple he had been a hero to the multitude, but a nonresisting prisoner on trial for his life could not be their hero. Calling him “⟦Q 185:5.6⟧the king of the Jews⟦/Q⟧” was an unwise move on Pilate’s part, for it wounded the pride of a people who were looking for a Messiah.
p185.s5.b3: At that very moment a message arrived from Claudia, urging him to have nothing to do with this innocent and just man. The letter only made Pilate hesitate further, and meanwhile the rulers moved among the crowd, urging the people to call for the release of Barabbas and the crucifixion of Jesus.
p185.s6.h: VI–VII. Pilate’s Last Appeal; Pilate’s Last Interview — “Behold the Man!”
p185.s6.b0: The text makes clear that those now gathered before Pilate were only Jesus’ enemies and a thoughtless crowd easily stirred up. Many of his friends either did not know of his arrest or were hiding in fear. Pilate had Jesus flogged in the hope of arousing pity — itself an illegal act before any sentence of death had been passed.
p185.s6.b1: The soldiers mocked him with a purple robe, a crown of thorns, and a reed. Pilate led him out, bloodstained, and declared again that he found no crime in him, but nothing could move hearts held captive by hatred and prejudice. When the high priest said that Jesus must die because he claimed to be the Son of God, Pilate grew more afraid than ever.
p185.s6.b4: Jesus told Pilate that he was not so guilty, since he was ignorant of the gospel; the one who betrayed him and those who delivered him had the greater sin. Pilate sought to release him, but Caiaphas warned that if he set this man free he was no friend of Caesar, and threatened to report him to the emperor. Fear for his own position overwhelmed every other consideration.
p185.s6.b5: Pilate was now pressed down by a double weight: a superstitious fear of Jesus himself and his fear of the Jewish leaders. Pointing to Jesus, he cried out in mockery, “⟦Q 185:7.5⟧Behold your king⟦/Q⟧!” and the chief priests and Sadducees publicly declared that they had no king but Caesar. The text records that even the thoughtless mob was shocked by these words.
p185.s7.h: VIII. Pilate’s Tragic Surrender — Washing the Hands Does Not Wash Away Responsibility
p185.s7.b0: The narrator sums up the whole trial in a single sentence: every step of proper procedure was missing.

head: Proper procedure
In the trial of Jesus
rows: A formal indictment
Arrested without a formal indictment
Evidence
Accused without evidence
Witnesses
Adjudged without witnesses
Punishment after sentence
Punished without a verdict
An impartial judge
Condemned by a judge who confessed he could find no fault in him

p185.s7.b2: Pilate feared a riot during the Passover, and he had recently been reprimanded by Caesar. He released Barabbas, then washed his hands in a basin and declared himself innocent of the blood of this man. But the text has already called him an unjust and fearful judge. The responsibility for a decision cannot be washed away with words.
p185.s8.b0: At the center of Paper 185 stands Pilate. He knew the truth, declared Jesus innocent more than once, and even looked for a way to release him. Yet because he feared for his position and his safety, he never did what was right. The paper shows that cowardice can produce greater injustice than malice.

p185.s8.b2: The next paper, Paper 186, “Just Before the Crucifixion,” describes the end of Judas and the Master’s attitude as he faced the cross.
p186.lead: The tragic end of Judas, the Master’s dignity throughout his trials, and the paper’s clear teaching that the death of Jesus was not a sacrifice.

p186.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p186.s0.h: Introduction — John Goes for the Master’s Mother
p186.s0.b0: Before he was taken to Herod, Jesus told John that there was nothing more he could do for him, and asked him to bring his mother to see him before he died. John was reluctant to leave his Master alone among his enemies, but he hurried off at once to Bethany, where Jesus’ family was gathered at the home of Martha and Mary.
p186.s0.b2: The family had reached Bethany only a few minutes before John arrived. Mary set out with John immediately, and Jesus’ sister Ruth, refusing to stay behind, followed along with her brother Jude. But by the time they reached the city, Jesus had already arrived at Golgotha. At James’s direction the rest of the family remained in Bethany, receiving news from David’s messengers.
p186.s1.h: I. The End of Judas Iscariot — The True Face of Sin
p186.s1.b0: About half past eight in the morning Pilate’s examination ended, and Jesus was handed over to the Roman soldiers. The high priest and his associates had returned to the temple’s hall of hewn stone to report to the Sanhedrin. Just then Judas appeared to claim his reward. Although his conscience had smitten him throughout the trial, he still expected to be praised before the council and to receive honors.
p186.s1.b1: Instead, a servant of the high priest called him out of the chamber and handed him a bag holding thirty pieces of silver, the current price of a good, healthy slave. Judas was stunned. He tried to go back in but was turned away by the doorkeeper. As if in a daze, he left the temple and wandered along with the crowds heading out to watch the crucifixion.
p186.s1.b2: When he saw from a distance the cross being raised, Judas rushed back to the temple, forced his way past the doorkeeper, and stood before the council, which was still in session. Nearly breathless, he stammered out a confession of his wrong and tried to return the money. His words came too late, but his remorse was real.

head: Stage
Judas’s state
rows: Expectation
He regarded his betrayal as a great service to the nation and expected praise and honor
Disillusionment
Paid thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave, he was humiliated and crushed
Remorse
Seeing the cross raised, he went back and confessed, “I have sinned in that I have betrayed innocent blood”
Rejection
The rulers mocked him and told him, in effect, “See to that yourself”
Despair
He threw the silver across the temple floor and took his own life in the valley of Hinnom

p186.s1.b5: In this scene the narrator lays bare the nature of sin. The glamor and intoxication of wrongdoing vanish, and the evildoer stands alone before the verdict of his own soul. What seemed an adventure in the committing now yields its harvest of plain facts.
p186.s1.b7: It is a heavy record: a man who had once been an ambassador of the kingdom of heaven ended his life forsaken and alone. It reads less as a condemnation of one person than as a warning of where self-centered calculation and nursed resentment can lead a human being.
p186.s2.h: II. The Master’s Attitude — When to Speak and When to Be Silent
p186.s2.b0: When he was arrested, Jesus knew that his work on earth in the flesh was finished, and he took little interest in the details of his trials. Yet he was not silent without exception. He always answered questions about the nature and divinity of his mission, whoever asked them, and he spoke when he thought a sincere person might learn more of the truth.

head: Before whom
Jesus’ attitude
rows: The servant of Annas
He suggested to the one who struck him that proper witnesses be called
The Sanhedrist court
He did not answer the false witnesses, but when asked whether he was the Son of God, he answered without hesitation
Herod
He firmly refused to speak before a curious and wicked king
Pilate
He spoke only when it might add to Pilate’s understanding of truth, and freely discussed the political charges that fell under his jurisdiction
Soldiers and servants
Mocked and struck, he showed patience and self-control, without resentment

p186.s2.b2: The text says that he had taught the futility of casting pearls before swine, and now he had the courage to practice it. His conduct joined the patient submission of human nature with the majestic silence of the divine. Nor did he try to change the outcome by persuasive eloquence, for he was convinced it was the Father’s will that he follow the natural course of human events.
p186.s2.b4: When the false testimony before Caiaphas had collapsed, Jesus answered the high priest’s question without hesitating, and so himself supplied the ground his enemies wanted. Truthful witness to his mission mattered more to him than protecting himself. Even when they blindfolded him, struck him in the face, and taunted him to prophesy, he did not become angry. His love for ignorant men was shown most clearly in just this patience and self-control.
p186.s2.b5: He was not interested in Pilate’s halfhearted efforts to release him, yet he pitied Pilate and tried to enlighten his darkened mind. The text records that the watching celestial hosts reported this trial to the universe as a scene of “⟦Q 186:2.6⟧Pilate on trial before Jesus.⟦/Q⟧”
p186.s2.b7: All his life Jesus never failed to reveal God to man, and now, in these final episodes and in his death, he made a new revelation of man to God. The few words he spoke during his trials were enough to show the whole universe what kind of character a human being can attain in partnership with God.
p186.s3.h: III. The Dependable David Zebedee — Keeping the News Moving
p186.s3.b0: When the temple guards went out to Gethsemane to arrest the followers, they found the camp deserted. David had expected the enemy to return and had moved some of the tents farther up the ravine; the guards burned the empty camp and went back. The Sanhedrin, satisfied that the followers had been thoroughly cowed, adjourned.
p186.s3.b1: Within five minutes of Jesus’ being handed over to the Roman soldiers, David’s messengers were on their way to Bethsaida, Pella, Sidon, Damascus, Alexandria, and elsewhere. All that day he sent messengers every half hour to bring news to the apostles, the Greeks, and Jesus’ family.
p186.s3.b2: David was the only one of the leading disciples who took literally Jesus’ statement that he would rise on the third day. Knowing the others did not expect it, he said little about his belief, but he quietly arranged for his messengers to gather at the home of Nicodemus early on Sunday morning. A simple and steady faith became the most practical preparation on the darkest of days.
p186.s3.b3: That the scattered community could follow events throughout that day was owing to the organization and faithfulness of this one man. Service of this kind, easily overshadowed by great events, shows what actually holds a community of faith together in a crisis.
p186.s4.h: IV. Preparation for the Crucifixion — The Son of Man Left Alone
p186.s4.b0: Pilate washed his hands in an effort to escape the guilt, yet in fact he delivered an innocent man to be crucified. The soldiers took off the robe Herod had put on Jesus and dressed him again in his own clothes; they mocked him, but inflicted no further physical abuse. His friends were now in hiding, his enemies had gone their way, and not even John was beside him.
p186.s4.b1: From the time he was handed over, a little after eight, until the procession started out shortly before nine, Jesus said nothing. The text tells us that during this time the executive business of a universe was virtually at a standstill. The soldiers began to be impressed by his composure, his dignity, and his uncomplaining silence. The departure was delayed because the captain decided at the last moment to take along two thieves already condemned to die. One of them had several times heard Jesus teach, both in the temple and at the Pella camp.
p186.s5.h: V. Jesus’ Death in Relation to the Passover — Not a Sacrifice
p186.s5.b0: It is true that Jesus died at about the time the Passover lambs were being slain in the temple, but the text states plainly that his death had nothing to do with the Jewish sacrificial system. The events that led to that hour show that his death was purely natural and man-managed.
p186.s5.b2: The Father did not interfere with the march of human events, but neither did he decree, demand, or require the death of his Son in this way. The experience needed for the bestowal had already been completed at his baptism; the manner of his later life and death was his personal ministry for the welfare of his creatures.

head: A common idea
What the text says
rows: Jesus’ death is bound up with the Passover sacrifice
There is no direct connection; the timing was coincidental (186:5.1)
God required the death of his Son
Man planned and carried it out; the Father did not require it (186:5.2)
His death atoned for the guilt of the race
Mankind has no racial guilt; guilt is a matter of personal, deliberate rebellion (186:5.7)
The gospel depends on Jesus’ death
The gospel was illuminated far more by his life than by his death (186:5.4)
The Father loves us more because of the bestowal
The Father’s love is unchanged; celestial intelligences came to know man in a new way (186:5.6)

p186.s5.b6: The text adds that sin and rebellion have nothing to do with the fundamental bestowal plan of the Sons of God; the plan of salvage appears only as an incidental feature of the bestowal. So when we look at the death of Jesus, the emphasis falls not on a transaction in which a price is paid but on the love he revealed in following the Father’s will to the end.
p186.s5.b7: Salvation would have been just as certain had Jesus not died at cruel hands. The love of God and the fact of sonship are relationships that have existed from eternity; they do not depend on the bestowal drama. Only one thing is needed to make them real in personal experience.
p186.s6.b0: Paper 186 lights the hours before the cross through three figures: Judas, who collapsed in despair; Jesus, who never lost his dignity; and David, who kept the news moving to the end. And it asks us not to see Jesus’ death as something God demanded, but to distinguish the deeds of men from the unchanging love of God.

head: Practice
The passage behind it
rows: Look past the allure of sin to its consequences
The harvest of the naked and unromantic facts (186:1.6)

He could not be intimidated (186:2.5)

David’s plan for Sunday morning (186:3.4)

Your spirit-born faith (186:5.9)

p186.s6.b2: The next paper, Paper 187, “The Crucifixion,” records the road to Golgotha and the final hours on the cross.
p187.lead: The road to Golgotha and five and a half hours on the cross: the Son of Man fulfilling the Father’s will to the end in forgiveness, care, and faith.

p187.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p187.s0.h: Introduction — A Life Laid Down Freely
p187.s0.b0: When the two brigands had been made ready, twelve soldiers under a centurion set out for the place of execution. This centurion was the very captain who had arrested Jesus in Gethsemane the night before. The two brigands were scourged according to custom, but the captain judged that Jesus had already suffered enough and ordered no further flogging. Because the two brigands were associates of Barabbas, the text observes that Jesus was crucified in Barabbas’s place.
p187.s0.b1: The narrator first makes clear that this death was a matter of Jesus’ own free will. In foretelling it, he had said that no one would take his life from him; he would lay it down of himself.
p187.s0.b3: Just before nine in the morning the procession left the governor’s headquarters. Among the crowd of some two hundred were a few secret sympathizers, but most were enemies or onlookers. Very few of the leaders went out to watch the execution; most of them were in the temple, discussing what to do about his followers.

p187.s1.h: I. On the Way to Golgotha — The Daughters of Jerusalem and Simon of Cyrene
p187.s1.b0: As was the custom, Jesus carried only the crossbeam on his shoulders. The captain walked ahead carrying the boards that named each man’s crime; on Jesus’ board Pilate had written in Latin, Greek, and Aramaic, “⟦Q 187:1.2⟧Jesus of Nazareth—the King of the Jews.⟦/Q⟧” The authorities begged him to change it, but Pilate refused: “⟦Q 187:1.3⟧What I have written, I have written.⟦/Q⟧”
p187.s1.b1: The text also records that crucifixion was not a Jewish mode of punishment. The Greeks and Romans had learned it from the Phoenicians, and it was never used on Roman citizens, only on slaves and subject peoples. The procession went by the most direct route out through the Damascus gate to Golgotha.
p187.s1.b2: In the narrow streets, tenderhearted women who had known Jesus’ comfort and love wept and lamented aloud. Since it was against the law to show sympathy for one condemned, they were brave indeed. Jesus was grateful for their sympathy, but he did not want them to draw the anger of the authorities, and he thought less of himself than of the troubles about to fall on Jerusalem.
p187.s1.b4: Jesus had neither eaten, drunk, nor slept since the Last Supper, and soon after passing the gate he fell under the weight of the crossbeam. The captain halted the soldiers and made Simon of Cyrene, who happened to be passing, carry the beam. Simon stayed through all those hours, and after the resurrection he became a valiant believer and led his family into the kingdom. Yet he never knew that the man whose burden he bore was the Jewish tutor who had once befriended his injured son.
p187.s1.b5: This record of a burden taken up by chance that changed a man and his whole family has a quiet power. Simon’s two sons, Alexander and Rufus, became effective teachers of the new gospel in Africa. A small kindness Jesus showed long before and the crossbeam Simon carried that day were joined, though neither man knew it.
p187.s2.b0: The soldiers bound Jesus’ arms to the crossbeam and nailed his hands and feet. The cross was not high; his feet were only about three feet from the ground, so he could see and hear every mocking word and face. There was considerable feeling against crucifixion in Jerusalem, and a society of Jewish women always sent someone with drugged wine to lessen the victim’s suffering. Jesus tasted it, but refused to drink.
p187.s2.b2: While the two brigands cursed their executioners, the only words Jesus spoke as he was nailed to the crossbeam were a plea for those who were nailing him. The text explains that a lifetime of unselfish service was the mainspring of that plea.
p187.s2.b4: The soldiers divided his clothes as was customary and cast lots for the seamless robe. The text says this was just as well: had his followers obtained his garments, they would have been tempted toward the worship of relics. Jesus wanted to leave behind nothing material, only the memory of a life dedicated to doing the Father’s will.
p187.s3.h: III. Those Who Saw the Crucifixion — Mockery and Silence
p187.s3.b0: The cross was raised about half past nine, and before eleven more than a thousand people had gathered. The unseen hosts of a universe watched in silence as the Creator underwent the most dishonorable of deaths at the hands of his creatures. Near the cross stood Mary his mother, Ruth, Jude, John, Salome, Mary Magdalene, and a group of earnest women believers.
p187.s3.b1: Passers-by and some of the rulers jeered that he had saved others but could not save himself. When Jesus made no reply, most of them went away, and the soldiers drank their sour wine and offered him mock toasts. When Jesus said, “I thirst,” the captain soaked a sponge in wine and moistened his lips.
p187.s4.h: IV. The Thief on the Cross — Faith at the Last Moment
p187.s4.b0: When one brigand railed at Jesus, the other thief, who had many times heard the Master teach, rebuked him. Jesus turned and smiled at him approvingly, and the man fanned the flickering flame of his faith and asked to be remembered when Jesus came into his kingdom.
p187.s4.b2: This young man had been led into a life of violence by those who praised robbery as a patriotic protest against injustice, and he had looked on Barabbas as a hero. Now he saw a true hero on the cross beside him. The text adds that anyone in the jeering crowd who had appealed to Jesus in faith would have been received with the same love. The door of salvation does not close even at the last moment.
p187.s4.b4: About noon, when John came back with Jesus’ mother and the women believers, Jesus entrusted his mother and John to each other and asked them to leave the scene. Mary spent the rest of her life in John’s home at Bethsaida. Even in his extreme suffering, Jesus did not forget to care for his family.
p187.s5.h: V. Last Hour on the Cross — “It Is Finished”
p187.s5.b0: After noon a sandstorm blowing in from the Arabian desert darkened the sky. Shortly after one o’clock Jesus began to lose human consciousness, and his human mind repeated passages from the Psalms. The words people heard — “⟦Q 187:5.2⟧My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?⟦/Q⟧” — were the opening line of the twenty-second Psalm, which he was reciting.
p187.s5.b1: This passage corrects an old misunderstanding. That cry was not the despair of one abandoned. Jesus never for a moment doubted that he had lived according to the Father’s will and was now laying down his life according to that will. As his consciousness faded, what held his mind were the scriptures he had learned since childhood.

p187.s5.b4: Seeing how Jesus died, the Roman centurion said that this was indeed a righteous man, and from that time he began to believe in Jesus. The text sums it up: Jesus died as royally as he had lived. He had provided for the safety of his apostles, restrained Peter’s violence, arranged for John to be near him, and at the last handed over his spirit to the Father.
p187.s5.b6: Because it was the day of preparation, the authorities asked Pilate to have the victims’ legs broken so the bodies could be taken down. Finding Jesus already dead, the soldiers pierced his side with a spear to make sure. A death that often took days came in less than five and a half hours, because of overwhelming emotional agony and spiritual anguish.
p187.s6.h: VI. After the Crucifixion — The Close of a Day of Sorrow
p187.s6.b0: About half past three David Zebedee sent out the last messengers announcing the Master’s death. John sent the women to the home of Elijah Mark and stayed at Golgotha until Joseph and Nicodemus came with the order to take the body. So ended a tragic day in which a vast universe shuddered at the indifference and perversity of mortals.
p187.s6.b1: Fewer than thirty people were present when the Master died: thirteen Roman soldiers and about fifteen believers, all of them women except Jude and John. In an hour when so many had scattered, the faithfulness of those who stayed to the end remains a shaft of light in this sorrowful record.
p187.s7.b0: Paper 187 focuses less on the description of suffering than on the character revealed in suffering. Jesus refused the wine that would dull his consciousness, forgave his executioners, received the repentant brigand, and cared for his mother. What came to light in that crisis were the motives and the love of a whole lifetime.

p187.s7.b2: The next paper, Paper 188, “The Time of the Tomb,” takes up the burial of Jesus, the hours in the tomb, and the meaning of the cross.
p188.lead: Thirty-six hours in Joseph’s tomb, and the true meaning of the death on the cross: not a ransom or atonement, but the climax of the Father’s love.

p188.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p188.s0.b0: The day and a half during which Jesus’ body lay in Joseph’s tomb is a chapter of Michael’s earth life that is almost unknown. The narrator says at the outset that the burial and the resurrection can be recorded, but what actually happened during the roughly thirty-six hours from three o’clock Friday afternoon to three o’clock Sunday morning cannot be told with certainty. This honesty — saying plainly what is not known — sets the tone of the whole paper.
p188.s0.b1: The authorities intended, as was customary, to throw Jesus’ body into the open burial pits of Gehenna. But Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus went to Pilate and asked for permission to give the body a proper burial. Joseph had brought a large sum of money to pay for the privilege, but Pilate would take nothing and signed the order at once.
p188.s1.h: I. The Burial of Jesus — The Courage of Two Former Sanhedrists
p188.s1.b0: At Golgotha, representatives of the Sanhedrin were standing by to make sure the body went to the criminal pits. When Joseph presented the order, they raised a tumult and tried to seize the body by force. The centurion had four soldiers stand over the body with drawn swords until order was restored; then he read Pilate’s permit aloud and gave the body to Joseph.
p188.s1.b2: A crucified person could not be buried in a Jewish cemetery, so the two men decided to lay Jesus in Joseph’s new family tomb, hewn out of solid rock. Joseph sincerely believed in the resurrection, while Nicodemus was doubtful. But these two former Sanhedrists, who had kept their faith more or less hidden, from this time on became the most outspoken disciples in Jerusalem.

p188.s1.b4: The men hurried away as the Sabbath approached, but Mary Magdalene, Mary the wife of Clopas, Martha (Jesus’ mother’s sister), and Rebecca of Sepphoris stayed near the tomb until it grew dark. The text adds that, apart from David Zebedee and Joseph, hardly any of the disciples really believed that Jesus would rise on the third day.
p188.s2.h: II. Safeguarding the Tomb — The Side That Remembered the Promise
p188.s2.b0: His followers had forgotten the promise of the third day, but his enemies had not. Gathering at the home of Caiaphas around midnight Friday, the leaders feared that the disciples might steal the body and proclaim a resurrection. The next morning a committee went to Pilate to ask for a guard.
p188.s2.b1: Pilate gave them ten soldiers, and they added ten temple guards, so that twenty men watched the tomb. Another stone was rolled before the tomb, and Pilate’s seal was set upon it. There is an irony here: the very thoroughness of their effort to defeat the promise would make the events that followed all the more clearly attested.
p188.s3.h: III. During the Sabbath Day — Thirty-Six Hours in the Tomb
p188.s3.b0: Throughout the Sabbath the disciples and apostles stayed in hiding, while nearly a million and a half pilgrims in Jerusalem talked about the crucifixion. These pilgrims would soon carry the news of the resurrection back to their homes. On Saturday night John Mark quietly gathered the eleven apostles in the upper room of the Last Supper.
p188.s3.b1: Meanwhile the scattered believers passed the Sabbath where they were. Mary returned with Ruth and Jude to the family at Bethany; David, at the home of Nicodemus, prepared to gather his messengers on Sunday morning; the women of Galilee stayed at Joseph’s home and prepared spices. Even in their grief, each quietly went on doing what he or she could.
p188.s3.b2: The narrator treats Jesus’ condition in the tomb with great care. Jesus said, “⟦Q 188:3.4⟧Father, into your hands I commend my spirit⟦/Q⟧,” yet since his Thought Adjuster had long since been personalized, the narrator admits not fully understanding what those words meant. He can only suggest that what Jesus entrusted to the Father was a spiritual reality analogous to the soul of faith-growing mortals.

p188.s3.b5: There is also a record that during this time the Supreme Council of Salvington met on Urantia and that messages passed between Michael and Immanuel. On the first mansion world, the “Michael memorial” was erected. The narrator says all this suggests that not all of Jesus’ personality was asleep, yet admits that its interpretation lies beyond his ability.
p188.s4.h: IV. Meaning of the Death on the Cross — Not Atonement or Ransom
p188.s4.b0: This section is the heart of the paper. The text states plainly that Jesus did not die to atone for the racial guilt of mankind, to appease an angry God, or to pay a ransom to Satan for man. At the same time it warns that in avoiding this error we must not lose sight of the true meaning of the death on the cross.
p188.s4.b2: The text says that before Jesus came one might perhaps have been justified in believing in such a stern God, but not since he lived and died among us. As revelation grows, our understanding of God must grow too. Its account of the nature of sin, in particular, lifts the vague sense of guilt so many people carry.

p188.s4.b5: What, then, is Jesus? The text says that while it may not be proper to call him a sacrificer or a ransomer, it is altogether proper to call him a savior. He lived and died not for this world alone but for a whole universe, and he forever made clear the survival of personality after death.
p188.s4.b7: Salvation is not a philosophic transaction but a reality. It rests on two realities, the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man, which can be grasped by faith and made part of one’s personal experience. The true believer is less concerned about future punishment than about present separation from God.
p188.s5.h: V. Lessons from the Cross — The Sign of Love Overcoming Hate
p188.s5.b0: The cross shows the supreme devotion of the true shepherd, even for unworthy members of his flock. It places the relationship between God and man forever on a family basis: God is the Father, and man is his son.
p188.s5.b2: The text says that the forgiveness of love transcends the forgiveness of mercy. Mercy sets guilt to one side, but love destroys sin and all the weakness that follows from it. Jesus’ forgiveness is not condonation that makes light of wrong; it is salvation from condemnation, which makes the wrong right.
p188.s5.b3: Jesus’ suffering was not confined to the cross. For more than twenty-five years he had carried the cross of a real and strenuous mortal existence. His prayer, “⟦Q 188:5.6⟧Father, forgive them,⟦/Q⟧” made the cross an eternal symbol of love triumphing over hate and of truth over evil. That loving devotion passed into his disciples: the first teacher to lay down his life for the gospel prayed, as he was stoned, that this sin not be laid to their charge.
p188.s5.b5: It is said that no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends, but Jesus’ love reached even to his enemies. The meaning of the cross, then, lies not in what the Father required but in what the Son willingly gave.
p188.s5.b7: The text urges us not to view the cross through the eyes of primitive man, assuming a God who is a relentless enforcer of law. Rather, it is the climax of the unfolding of the Father’s divine love. It also gives the comfort that no one need ever fear that the Creator does not know our suffering.
p188.s5.b9: The narrator sums up once more: the death on the cross was not meant to reconcile man to God. It was meant to stimulate man’s realization of the Father’s eternal love and the Son’s unending mercy, and to broadcast these truths to a whole universe. The record that creatures on countless worlds, ready to give up the struggle of faith, looked at Jesus on the cross and rose again shows that this love is still a power that lifts the weary.
p188.s6.b0: Along with the quiet faithfulness at the tomb, Paper 188 asks us to change the way we see the cross. It is not an offering to appease an angry God; it is the sign of a good person giving himself to the wicked and saving them by love. To look upon it stirs in us the desire to go and do likewise.
